about: How large an object has to be before a deploy finding is worth more attention than the same finding on a small one. Written for this package from the shape of the operations themselves; no threshold table was copied from another linter or vendor document. These are HEURISTICS and the numbers say so: the same rewrite that is invisible at ten thousand rows is an outage at half a billion, and no single number separates those cleanly for every schema, disk and maintenance window. What the artefact buys is that the number is a reviewable line in a diff rather than a constant somebody once typed into a class. A threshold never creates a finding and never removes one — it only raises the severity of a finding that already exists, and every raise is reported as resting on an estimate.

rewrite.about: The table is rewritten in place: every row copied, the whole time under a lock nothing else can read through. Cost scales with SIZE rather than with row count, because what is copied is bytes.

index_build.about: An index is built over an existing table. Concurrent builds do not block writes but take longer and can fail part-way; the blocking form holds the table for the duration. Row count is the better predictor here — the work is per row, not per byte.

constraint_validation.about: An existing constraint is validated against existing rows. Cheaper than a rewrite because nothing is copied, and still a full scan — so it is the same shape of risk one step down.

backfill.about: Data is written by the migration itself. This is the operation the guidance is sharpest about: a backfill that belongs in a queued job looks identical to one that belongs in a migration until somebody knows how many rows it touches. That is why the recommendation is deliberately unarmed without statistics and armed by them.
